extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of religious criticism/skepticism (readers of Thomas Paine)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative criteria used to judge the authenticity, authorship, and truthfulness of Biblical prophetic books and prophets; the page applies these criteria to Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, Jonah, and other prophetic texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fulfilment of specified prophecy timeframe
rubrics_metrics.description: A prophecy that includes a limited time for its completion must be fulfilled within that time (e.g., Isaiah’s sign: 'before this child shall know to refuse the evil, and choose the good' — the promise must be completed before that event).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a later writer or interpreter applies a time-limited sign to an event centuries later (as Matthew applies Isaiah’s sign to Jesus), that is a perversion and indicates falsity. Example: Isaiah’s sign was immediate; applying it seven hundred years later is invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal scope appropriate to prophetic role
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophecy in the Old Testament originally concerned immediate or near events ('things of the time then passing') rather than distant future ages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpreting poetical or local predictions as forecasts of remote future events (e.g., using them to justify New Testament claims) is improper. True prophetic statements should match the time-frame suggested by their language and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal consistency and coherent narrative order
rubrics_metrics.description: A genuine authored book should have coherent historical sequence and not repeat the same events in contradictory ways or restart the narrative without cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of the same events being 'several times repeated...sometimes in contradiction' and chapters that 'begin anew, and end abruptly' indicates the book is a medley of unconnected anecdotes and not the work of a single, sane author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of ascribed authorship (internal evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: The text should contain internal evidence consistent with authorship by the person to whom it is ascribed; absence of such evidence or presence of anachronisms argues against authenticity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If internal details show the book could not have been written by the named author (as Paine argues for Moses, Joshua, Samuel, etc.), treat authorship as doubtful and consider later compilation by 'book-makers.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Falsifiability and conditional provisos
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophetic statements that include conditional provisos (e.g., 'if that nation...turn from their evil, I will repent me') render the prophecy non-falsifiable and therefore unreliable as true prediction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provisions that allow a prediction to be reversed depending on the subject's behavior provide a 'door to escape' for the prophet and make him impossible to prove wrong; this is an anti-pattern for genuine prophecy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of partisan/party motive
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophets frequently acted as party agents, prophesying for or against a political faction; prophetic content aligning with party interests suggests partisan motive rather than divine insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When prophecy systematically supports one side (e.g., Judah vs Israel), treat it as political poetry or propaganda rather than objective revelation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of deliberate manufacture or staged signs
rubrics_metrics.description: The possibility that prophets engineered signs (e.g., finding or arranging for a pregnant girl to fulfil a sign) indicates fraud rather than supernatural sanction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims of miraculous or prophetic signs should be scrutinized for natural or human fabrication; Paine suggests prophets could 'take measures to make this sign appear.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Contradiction with historical events
rubrics_metrics.description: When a prophet’s declared outcome is contradicted by subsequent historical events (e.g., Isaiah’s assurance vs. the later success of the kings against Ahaz; Jeremiah’s predictions about Zedekiah), the prophecy is false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use independent historical record (where available) to check prophetic claims; clear contradiction is grounds to reject prophetic veracity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral and behavioural consistency of the prophet
rubrics_metrics.description: A prophet’s own conduct—lying, prevaricating, acting as a partisan, or seeking personal advantage—undermines claims of divine inspiration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Jeremiah alleged to prevaricate before princes; prophets who lie to serve political ends. Ethical failings of the prophet are taken as evidence against prophetic legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary form indicates poet/performer rather than seer
rubrics_metrics.description: The original Hebrew role of 'prophet' often meant poet or performer (music/poetry); prophetic books written in poetic language may be literary/ritual works rather than records of genuine seership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the text's style, mention of musical instruments, and poetic tropes dominate, classify it as poetic composition (poet/performer) not necessarily as genuine forecasting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dreams and visions as coded contemporaneous communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Accounts of dreams and visions may have been an obscure or metaphorical method for political prisoners to convey plans or opinions, not literal supernatural revelations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret visionary passages (especially from Ezekiel and Daniel) as possible ciphers for immediate political concerns of captives; the presence of obscure metaphorical language is consistent with encryption for insiders, not universal prophecy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency toward fabulous or satirical content
rubrics_metrics.description: Narratives involving improbable miracles or fantastical elements (e.g., Jonah swallowed by a fish, improbable gourd growth) are better read as fable, satire, or allegory than literal history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When stories read as contrivances or moral fables, treat them as literary devices meant to satirize or teach, not as reliable historical miracles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composite authorship / editorial 'book-maker' indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: A book that appears to be 'a medley of detached unauthenticated anecdotes' with repetitions and contradictions suggests later compilation by editors rather than single-author work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signs like abrupt topic shifts, repeated events with differing detail, and incoherent sequencing point to redactional compilation; such books should not be treated as coherent original works by the ascribed prophet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of prophetic content to likely audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophetic messages should suit the actual situation of the supposed prophet and his contemporaries; content that better fits political or local circumstances argues against long-range prophetic intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the prophecy’s most natural interpretation addresses immediate military, political, or personal circumstances (e.g., advice about surrender in a siege), favor that reading over anachronistic messianic applications.
